title: The Taliban’s Next Five Years
gist: Five years after seizing power, the Taliban have proven surprisingly stable — reduced conflict, ~5 percent GDP growth, and quasi-normalized regional diplomacy — but Michael Kugelman sees the next five years as riskier given a new armed resistance movement, resilient ISK, and rising tension with Pakistan; the brief also flags a major U.S. policy break on Kashmir and worsening Bangladesh-India relations.

insights.claim: The World Bank estimated Afghanistan's real annual GDP growth at nearly 5 percent this year, driven partly by the Taliban's success generating revenue through customs duties and tax collection and by robust trade with Central Asian neighbors, despite the loss of foreign assistance that long propped up the economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence the Taliban have built functioning fiscal-extraction capacity (customs/tax) independent of foreign aid — relevant for assessing regime durability and Afghanistan's role in Central Asian trade corridors.

insights.claim: Afghanistan has not been at war since the August 2021 U.S. withdrawal, a first in four decades, and terrorist attacks have declined following Taliban offensives against Islamic State-Khorasan (IS-K), though this does not mean the country is secure for women, religious minorities, and dissidents.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A reduction in open warfare (though not human-rights conditions) is the key metric behind the Taliban's stability narrative — relevant baseline for tracking any resurgence in conflict as a regime-destabilization signal.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'By some measures, security has improved'

insights.claim: Nearly 20 countries still operate diplomatic representations in Kabul, Taliban diplomats have taken up posts in many Asian capitals, and the group was invited to the 2024 UN climate summit — meaning the international community has effectively accepted Taliban rule as a reality even while withholding formal recognition (only Russia formally recognizes the Taliban government).
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: De facto international normalization without de jure recognition is a durable status quo — relevant for assessing Afghanistan-linked trade, transit, and investment flows even absent formal diplomatic recognition by most Western governments.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The Taliban may be isolated'

insights.claim: Sami Sadat, a pre-Taliban senior military officer, launched a new armed campaign against the Taliban this month via his Afghanistan United Front; the movement will struggle without external sponsorship, but continued global economic shocks could worsen living conditions and boost recruitment to the resistance.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A new organized armed opposition movement is a nascent but trackable tail risk to Taliban regime stability, contingent on economic conditions and potential external sponsorship — worth monitoring for escalation.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Earlier this month, Sami Sadat'

insights.claim: A grenade attack near a Kabul school in a Hazara (Shiite minority) neighborhood is a reminder that IS-K, described as notoriously resilient, or groups allied with it, could resurge, while tensions with former sponsor Pakistan — which accuses the Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants and has carried out several rounds of cross-border strikes over the last year — could explode into open conflict.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Two concurrent, independent security risks (IS-K resurgence and Pakistan cross-border conflict escalation) both threaten Taliban stability in the next five years — relevant for regional security-risk forecasting and Afghanistan-Pakistan border trade disruption.

themes.theme: U.S. breaks decades of Kashmir neutrality

insights.claim: U.S. ambassador to India Sergio Gor declared that Kashmir is 'an important part of India' and said his government would consider easing U.S. travel warnings to the region — comments that appear to endorse India's position on the Kashmir dispute, breaking many years of U.S. policy refraining from taking a position, and contradicting Trump's own prior public offer to help find a 'solution' in Kashmir.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A concrete, on-record U.S. policy shift toward endorsing India's Kashmir position is a notable geopolitical signal that could affect U.S.-Pakistan relations and India-Pakistan tension dynamics — worth tracking for further U.S. statements or a formal travel-warning change.

insights.claim: Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is delaying travel to India for the 2026 BRICS leaders' summit pending a more 'conducive environment,' after India's platforming of exiled former PM Sheikh Hasina (sentenced to death in absentia last November) at a New Delhi event infuriated Dhaka; Bangladesh has demanded India extradite Hasina and hand over two men accused of a deadly attack on activist Osman Hadi.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A concrete diplomatic rupture risks Bangladesh's planned BRICS engagement and broader India-Bangladesh economic relations — relevant for regional trade and BRICS-summit attendance risk tracking.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Last week, Bangladeshi Prime Minister'

insights.claim: India is unlikely to extradite Hasina given New Delhi's deep ties to her and her family, but it may be willing to consider handing over the two men accused in the Osman Hadi attack — a partial concession that could serve as a de-escalation signal.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable near-term prediction (partial concession on the Hadi case but not extradition) useful for tracking India-Bangladesh relationship trajectory.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Because of its deep ties to Hasina'
